content: Lactic acid bacteria (LAB) are a group of Gram-positive bacteria that are characterized by their low guanine-cytosine (GC) content in their DNA, their ability to tolerate acidic environments, and their non-sporulating, non-respiring nature. These bacteria are either rod-shaped (bacilli) or spherical (cocci) and are commonly found in decomposing plant material and dairy products. LAB are notable for producing lactic acid as the primary metabolic byproduct during carbohydrate fermentation. This acid production plays a critical role in food preservation by inhibiting the growth of spoilage organisms and pathogens. Additionally, many LAB strains produce protein-based antimicrobial compounds called bacteriocins, which further enhance their ability to suppress undesirable microorganisms. The metabolic byproducts of LAB, including lactic acid, contribute significantly to the flavor, texture, and overall sensory qualities of fermented foods. LAB are widely used in the food industry and are considered safe for consumption, as evidenced by their generally regarded as safe (GRAS) status. They are also important for maintaining healthy microbial communities on human mucosal surfaces. The core genera of LAB include Lactobacillus, Leuconostoc, Pediococcus, Lactococcus, and Streptococcus, with additional genera such as Aerococcus, Carnobacterium, Enterococcus, Oenococcus, Tetragenococcus, Vagococcus, and Weissella also classified within the LAB group. These bacteria belong to the order Lactobacillales. LAB are uniquely adapted to thrive in acidic environments, which gives them a competitive advantage during natural fermentation processes. Their ability to tolerate low pH levels is due to their production of organic acids, such as lactic acid. In laboratory settings, LAB are typically cultured on media containing carbohydrates, as most species lack the ability to respire and rely on fermentation for energy production. The metabolism of LAB can be classified into two main types based on their hexose fermentation pathways: homolactic fermentation and heterolactic fermentation. Homolactic LAB, such as Lactococcus, Enterococcus, Streptococcus, Pediococcus, and group I Lactobacilli, utilize the Embden-Meyerhof-Parnas (EMP) pathway. In this pathway, one molecule of glucose is converted into two molecules of pyruvate, which are then reduced to lactic acid to maintain redox balance. This process generates two molecules of ATP per glucose molecule. In contrast, heterofermentative LAB, such as Leuconostoc, Oenococcus, Weissella, and group III Lactobacilli, use the pentose phosphate pathway (also known as the phosphoketolase pathway). In this pathway, glucose-6-phosphate is converted into 6-phosphogluconate and then decarboxylated to produce carbon dioxide and pentose-5-phosphate. The pentose-5-phosphate is split into glyceraldehyde phosphate (GAP) and acetyl phosphate, which are further metabolized into lactic acid and ethanol, respectively. This process produces ATP and other end products in equimolar amounts. In 1985, the genus Streptococcus underwent reclassification based on biochemical and molecular characteristics. This reclassification resulted in the creation of new genera, including Lactococcus, Enterococcus, and Vagococcus, in addition to Streptococcus. Historically, streptococci were classified based on serological methods, which have been found to align well with modern taxonomic definitions. Lactococci, formerly known as Lancefield group N streptococci, are extensively used as starter cultures in dairy fermentations. Humans are estimated to consume approximately 10^18 lactococci annually. Two subspecies of Lactococcus lactis, namely L. lactis subsp. lactis and L. lactis subsp. cremoris, are widely used in the production of soft and hard cheeses, respectively. These strains are also model organisms for LAB research. The genome of L. lactis subsp. lactis strain IL1403 was sequenced in 2001, marking a significant milestone in LAB genomics and advancing our understanding of their applications. Bacteriophage contamination poses a significant challenge in the industrial fermentation of food products, chemicals, and biotechnological products. The large-scale cultivation of LAB in fermentation vats creates an environment where bacteriophages can rapidly infect and disrupt bacterial cultures, leading to economic losses. The interaction between bacteriophages and their bacterial hosts is a critical area of study in the food fermentation industry. Phages attach to bacterial cells via receptor-binding proteins (RBPs), which recognize specific receptors on the bacterial surface. These receptors may include polysaccharides, teichoic acids, or membrane proteins. Once attached, phages must penetrate the thick peptidoglycan layer of Gram-positive LAB to inject their genetic material. This process is facilitated by peptidoglycan-degrading enzymes, which are structural components of many LAB phages. The dairy industry has long recognized the threat of phage contamination and has collaborated with researchers and starter culture companies to develop strategies to mitigate phage propagation and evolution. LAB are also widely used as probiotics, which are live microorganisms that confer health benefits when consumed in adequate amounts. Probiotics aim to deliver beneficial bacteria to the gut ecosystem, while prebiotics are non-digestible carbohydrates that serve as substrates for beneficial gut bacteria. LAB, particularly members of the genera Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium, are among the most extensively studied probiotic organisms. These bacteria play a crucial role in promoting gut health and maintaining a balanced microbial community in the gastrointestinal tract.
